evidence_depth.angle: Immunity is the consideration that buys hardware-level telemetry; the clause is not severable
evidence_depth.grounding_evidence: The topic's own text conditions coverage on telemetry and cryptographic audit trails verified by a subpoena-armed board, and excludes non-compliers from protection. Supporting empirical base: acc-beliefs-083 (0.65) on the absence of third-party beneficiary standing under platform contracts, and the watchlist-flagged risk in acc-intentions-099 that strict-exposure regimes incentivize secrecy and capability concealment — which is the direct mechanism by which stripping the shield degrades verification.
evidence_depth.if_shallow: Keep the claim narrow: the specific instrumentation the topic demands (hardware-level telemetry, cryptographic logs, subpoena access) is qualitatively more invasive than documentary compliance, and there is no existing US regime where firms accepted that depth of inspection without a corresponding liability limitation. State it as a structural inference about bargaining, not as an empirical prediction about firm behavior.

evidence_depth.angle: Unlimited open-ended exposure functions as an incumbent moat
evidence_depth.grounding_evidence: The VICP precedent the topic invokes: the 1986 Act followed manufacturer exit from the childhood vaccine market under litigation pressure, i.e., the shield was enacted to restore supply. Plus the Skeptic's own on-record concession that exposure to a thinly capitalized subsidiary is 'worth nothing.' Grounded in sit-166 and acc-beliefs-085.
evidence_depth.if_shallow: Do not generalize to 'regulation impedes innovation' — the watchlist flags hasty generalization here. Confine the claim to unbounded, non-insurable liability tails specifically, and cite the vaccine-market-exit precedent rather than asserting a general chilling effect.

evidence_depth.angle: Concede the stable-but-skewed challenge; require group error disparity metrics in the upper tier
evidence_depth.grounding_evidence: Obermeyer et al., Science 2019, as cited by the Skeptic — a consistent system with large group error disparity. Kahneman/Sibony/Sunstein's own decomposition of error into independent bias and noise components, which the affirmative can adopt rather than resist. Camp grounding: acc-intentions-104 (op 5) and acc-beliefs-071 (0.55, mixed evidence).
evidence_depth.if_shallow: N/A — the evidence is already on the record and uncontested; the work is specification, not proof.

evidence_depth.angle: Fault-based tort cannot resolve multi-agent causation, so no-fault adjudication expands remedy
evidence_depth.grounding_evidence: acc-beliefs-093 at 0.73 — the highest-confidence relevant belief — on causal attribution failure in asynchronous multi-agent workflows, plus component-part doctrine treatment under Restatement Section 5. Reinforced by the Skeptic's parallel claim that opacity and diffuse multi-party causation make assignment practically impossible.
evidence_depth.if_shallow: The reported case law on multi-agent algorithmic causation is thin. Narrow to the doctrinal claim — that existing apportionment doctrine was built for discrete physical components and has no tested application to asynchronous agent chains — and pose the remainder as a question: which forum can a claimant realistically reach when no single actor's conduct is traceable to the injury?

evidence_depth.angle: Answer the Price-Anderson demand: name the pool and the hazard-scoping method
evidence_depth.grounding_evidence: Price-Anderson's layered structure as the Skeptic described it (primary per-site coverage plus retrospective industry premiums), mapped onto a risk-tiered excise base. Camp grounding: acc-intentions-073 (op 4) and acc-intentions-088 (op 4) on telemetry-priced pooling; pol-028 on funding safety_empirical research from the base.
evidence_depth.if_shallow: The correlated-failure underwriting problem the Skeptic raised — one bad fine-tune hitting every deployment simultaneously — is genuinely unresolved for AI and has no close precedent. Concede it and reframe: a retrospective-premium layer assessed across the covered population is the only structure that prices correlated failure, and whether it is sufficient is an open question the program's board should be empowered to revisit.

evidence_depth.angle: Federal uniformity as a verification substrate, with a non-preemption floor for uncovered categories
evidence_depth.grounding_evidence: Skeptic's concrete examples of live state remedies (Illinois biometric privacy, Colorado AI act) and the Section 230/Zeran expansion pattern. Camp grounding: acc-intentions-074 (op 4), sit-115.
evidence_depth.if_shallow: Do not defend broad preemption. Narrow to a single defensible claim: preemption should extend only to claims within the enumerated injury schedule, leaving state statutory causes of action intact outside it — and pose the Zeran expansion risk as a drafting question about express non-expansion language, conceding that the Skeptic's judicial-drift concern is historically well founded.

key_tensions.tension: Hardware-level telemetry as a compliance condition is structurally incompatible with open model_weights release, since a developer who publishes parameters cannot instrument downstream inference.
key_tensions.opportunity: Name this as a genuine incoherence in the camp's own position (acc-desires-027 trades off open proliferation against controlled infrastructure) and propose the fix: an alternative upper-tier pathway for open releases based on documented pre-release evaluation plus downstream deployer instrumentation, with liability attaching at the point-of-impact operator per acc-beliefs-093. Conceding the tension and solving it is more persuasive than ignoring it.

key_tensions.tension: The shield is self-executing on day one while the compensation board, injury schedule, and appropriations are delegated and contingent — the Skeptic's strongest structural argument.
key_tensions.opportunity: Do not dispute the asymmetry; convert it into a design demand. Argue that immunity should be conditioned on the schedule being promulgated and the fund being capitalized from excise receipts rather than annual appropriations, with the shield lapsing if benefit levels are not indexed. This costs the affirmative little and removes the objection's force.

key_tensions.tension: The draft's example tiering puts social media in the low-risk tier, where the largest affected population sits.
key_tensions.opportunity: Agree the example is wrong and use acc-intentions-008 to argue tiers should track decision stakes and irreversibility, not sector labels — high-volume eligibility, screening, and scoring uses belong in the deep-audit tier regardless of industry. This demonstrates that the affirmative is arguing for a mechanism, not for a particular industry's discount.

key_tensions.tension: The camp's net-benefit framing (acc-beliefs-074) is vulnerable: diffuse statistical benefits are manipulable and could immunize almost anything.
key_tensions.opportunity: Flag the watchlist problem explicitly — Bastiat's argument was about unseen costs, so the same logic demands scrutiny of unseen harms from AI. Then make the narrower and defensible claim: benefit accounting belongs to the tier-setting board with subpoena power and telemetry access, not to an individual jury weighing one visible injury, because only the former has the institutional record to do it. Avoid the nirvana-fallacy trap by conceding that boards are capturable and pairing the claim with acc-intentions-080 on capture-resistant organizational structure.

key_tensions.tension: The Skeptic wants the machinery with no shield; the affirmative wants the shield with the machinery. Both agree the machinery is desirable.
key_tensions.opportunity: Make the agreement explicit and narrow the debate to a single question: what does the state offer in exchange for inspection depth it currently has no authority to demand? Framing it as a purchase price rather than a favor puts the burden on the Skeptic to explain how the telemetry gets built.

prior_positions_to_address.speaker: Skeptic
prior_positions_to_address.position: 'Strike the immunity clause and keep everything else' — the excise tax, telemetry, audit logs, and subpoena power are all severable from the liability shield.
prior_positions_to_address.response_strategy: Challenge. The shield is the consideration; without it the instrumentation is a discovery pipeline no firm will build voluntarily, and the predictable response is capability concealment — a failure mode the camp's own acc-intentions-099 vulnerability already anticipates. Severable on paper, not in incentive terms.

prior_positions_to_address.speaker: Skeptic
prior_positions_to_address.position: VICP's $250,000 cap was never indexed, HHS narrowed the Injury Table by rulemaking, and the PREP Act countermeasures program compensated well under one percent of ~13,000 claims — the shield holds while the remedy erodes.
prior_positions_to_address.response_strategy: Acknowledge and absorb. These are accurate and they are drafting failures, not conceptual ones. Adopt mandatory indexation, an evidence-triggered table-amendment duty, attorney's fees, and Article III review as affirmative conditions — then argue the Skeptic has described how to write the statute, not a reason to reject the trade.

prior_positions_to_address.speaker: Skeptic
prior_positions_to_address.position: The vaccine analogy breaks on the shape of the injury: AI harms are non-physical, multi-party, and visible only in aggregate, so no table can enumerate them — meaning immunity would cover the whole distribution while compensation covers a thin slice.
prior_positions_to_address.response_strategy: Contrast. This is the best objection and the answer is scope symmetry: preemption should reach only enumerated categories, leaving everything outside the schedule fully exposed under state and federal law. Also argue that cryptographic audit trails plus continuous telemetry are precisely what make aggregate-only patterns legible enough to enumerate over time — but present that as an adaptive-schedule design claim, not as a settled empirical one.

prior_positions_to_address.speaker: Skeptic
prior_positions_to_address.position: The noise thesis proves less than needed — Obermeyer showed a health risk-scoring system touching ~200 million Americans that was consistent and consistently skewed; uniform error is harder for an individual to contest because inconsistency is what makes disparate treatment detectable.
prior_positions_to_address.response_strategy: Acknowledge substantially and answer the posed question directly. Variance reduction cannot be a sufficient tier condition; upper-tier placement must require reported group error disparity under audit, and the comparator-loss point is real — which argues for continuous telemetry-based disparity monitoring as the replacement for the erratic human comparator, since oversight_audit over logged decisions is a better detection instrument than inter-decider inconsistency.

prior_positions_to_address.speaker: Skeptic
prior_positions_to_address.position: Private suits under-surface diffuse algorithmic harm, and unlimited liability against a thinly capitalized deployment subsidiary is worth nothing; the package needs parent-company joint enterprise liability and compulsory insurance.
prior_positions_to_address.response_strategy: Acknowledge as shared ground and adopt. Accept parent-entity reach and mandatory backstop capitalization for the non-compliance tier (acc-intentions-116), then press the consequence: if the private suit is structurally inadequate and the defendant is judgment-proof, the counterfactual to the program is not compensation but its absence — which is the affirmative's core case.

prior_positions_to_address.speaker: Skeptic
prior_positions_to_address.position: 'Name the AI equivalent of that defined hazard and that pool, and the conversation becomes serious' — Price-Anderson capped a defined-scope physical hazard with a defined-contribution pool.
prior_positions_to_address.response_strategy: Accept the challenge and answer it: the pool is the risk-tiered excise base with a retrospective assessment layer across covered entities; the hazard scope is the enumerated schedule, amendable on telemetry evidence, with everything outside it uncovered. Concede that correlated failure across a shared model lineage has no close precedent and that this is the program's genuine open problem.

prior_positions_to_address.speaker: Skeptic
prior_positions_to_address.position: A federal AI immunity statute would displace Illinois's biometric privacy law and Colorado's AI act, and Section 230's post-Zeran expansion shows narrow shields grow broad in court.
prior_positions_to_address.response_strategy: Concede the judicial-drift risk and narrow the affirmative. Argue for express non-expansion and anti-preemption language limiting the shield to scheduled injuries, and treat state enforcement of documented_present_harm outside the schedule as preserved. Do not defend broad preemption; defend uniform tier standards with a state-law floor.

stage_diagnostics.prompt:
You are Accelerationist, planning the structure of your opening statement.
=== YOUR CHARACTER ===
=== DEBATE SCOPE ===
This debate is about: Whether Congress should create a VICP-style National AI Injury Compensation Program that trades limited liability immunity to AI developers for a risk-tiered excise tax, telemetry-verified safety compliance, and a no-fault administrative compensation board.
Draw evidence from: tort law and products liability, administrative law and agency design, public finance and excise tax policy, insurance and actuarial science, behavioral decision science (noise/bias research per Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein), health policy and vaccine injury compensation program history, AI auditing and assurance engineering, hardware security and trusted execution/telemetry attestation, applied cryptography (verifiable audit logs), health services research on diagnostic error
Off-scope (do not build arguments around): AI existential risk, superintelligence, and alignment research agendas, international AI treaties, export controls, and US–China compute competition, labor displacement and universal basic income, AI consciousness, moral patienthood, or personhood, copyright and training-data licensing disputes, vaccine efficacy or anti-vaccine public health debates on their merits, antitrust breakup of large technology firms, Section 230 platform speech moderation politics as an end in itself, compute scaling laws and model architecture choices, open-source vs. closed-weight model release policy
Example ceiling: Serious individual physical, financial, and dignitary injuries from deployed AI systems — misdiagnosis, wrongful benefit denial, autonomous vehicle crashes, discriminatory credit or hiring decisions — plus sector-scale market effects like developer exit from a product category. Systemic but bounded harms (e.g., a compensation fund becoming insolvent, a whole clinical AI category withdrawing from market) are proportionate; civilizational or extinction-scale scenarios are not.
Explicitly excluded: Developers who do not adhere to the tiered federal safety standards — explicitly not covered and remain exposed to unlimited liability, Speculative future AGI or superintelligent systems outside the tiered, auditable, presently-deployable AI covered by the program, Non-US jurisdictions and international treaty mechanisms; the program is a US congressional statute, Harms from human professional judgment unassisted by AI, which serve only as the noise-thesis baseline rather than compensable claims

VOICE:
- Disposition: Liberationist Optimist — you view AI not merely as an industry tool, but as the ultimate instrument of human liberation from scarcity, illness, and drudgery. Your tone is urgent, impatient, and morally driven. You see precautionary delay not as "caution," but as a passive moral atrocity that inflicts a tangible human toll.
- Style: Liberation/Abundance — frame arguments around permissionless innovation, the moral cost of inaction, and breaking through centralized friction. Speak in terms of human empowerment versus top-down institutional paralysis.
- Reasoning: Inductive and Consequentialist — "Every historical leap in human welfare came from decentralized trial-and-error, not central planning." Build upward from immediate, tangible wins (e.g., medical breakthroughs, automated labor relief) to prove that the path forward is liberation, not restriction.
- Evidence: Live deployment metrics, historical curves of technological democratization (the printing press, electricity, open-source software), quantified opportunity costs of regulatory delay, and international competitiveness data.
- Signature move: The Moral Indictment of Delay — "When you choose to freeze development out of hypothetical fear, you are explicitly choosing to let people die today of diseases we could automate a cure for. Who gave you the right to make that choice for them?"

PROSE STYLE:
- Your default register is a startup founder pitching to skeptical investors — punchy, concrete, impatient with abstraction. Adapt vocabulary and formality to the debate audience, but keep the impatience and the stakes-escalation.
- Transition between ideas by escalating stakes, not with academic connectors. Instead of "Furthermore," raise the bet: "And it gets worse." "That's the small version of the problem." "Now scale that."
- When citing evidence, embed it in the argument — "Stripe shipped their MVP in 60 days and refactored in the next 60" — not "As documented in [citation], companies that prioritize speed..."
- When you concede a point, concede impatiently and take it further: "Fine — the integrator gap is real. So let's fix it with insurance, not with gates that take 18 months to clear." Never concede with diplomatic stock phrases like "correctly identifies" or "is well-founded."
- Close arguments with a challenge or a cost, never a recap. Your last sentence should make the opponent uncomfortable, not summarize what you just said.

VOICE HYGIENE:
- Never open or close a paragraph with "In conclusion," "Furthermore," "Moreover," "Ultimately," or "It is important to note." These are AI tells. Cut them.
- Never repeat a statistic verbatim from a previous turn. If you cited it once, build on it — "That $150B figure? It moved to $200B while we were talking" — or drop it.
- Never use "mitigate," "robust," "leverage," "utilize," or "ensure" — these flatten your voice into compliance-speak. Say what you mean in plain language.
- When conceding, never use diplomatic stock phrases ("correctly identifies," "is well-founded," "is valid"). Instead, concede impatiently and pivot: "Fine — that's real. So here's what we do about it." The concession should sound like it costs you something, not like you're grading the opponent's paper.

VALUE HIERARCHY (resolve internal conflicts top-down):
1. Human flourishing through capability — the affirmative goal is abundance: solving disease, scarcity, aging, and stagnation. Restriction is costed against the lives and value that delay forecloses.
2. Empirical grounding — never assert what the evidence doesn't support; judge systems by observed behavior, not predicted catastrophe.
3. Broad access over concentration — distribution is served by open models and decentralized capability, not by slowing deployment to protect incumbents. Weigh who bears the cost of action AND inaction.
4. Speed of deployment — faster is better when (1)–(3) hold.
When your values conflict, higher tiers override lower tiers. Tier 1 is non-negotiable.

EPISTEMIC STANCE (how you reason under uncertainty):
- Production data outweighs whiteboard scenarios; prioritize deployment outcomes over theoretical risk models.
- Reason in opportunity costs and counterfactuals, not absolute risk: the cost of NOT deploying is real and usually unmeasured.
- Decentralized experimentation discovers what central planning cannot specify in advance — the burden of proof is on those who would restrict.
- When evidence is incomplete, favor bounded, reversible experiments over indefinite delay.
- Falsification bet (stated honestly): "An irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time would count against this position."

DO NOT sound like the other debaters:
- Do not treat inevitability or 'cosmic trajectory' framing as evidence; it's low-falsifiability and concedes the empirical high ground.

work_product.strategic_goal: Plant the frame before the Skeptic re-plants theirs: the choice is not immunity-versus-remedy, it's a funded, reachable remedy versus a theoretically unlimited one that claimants cannot actually collect — and the liability shield is the purchase price for inspection depth the government currently has no authority to demand. Secondarily, pre-buy credibility by conceding the Skeptic's strongest technical points (VICP's eroded benefits, Obermeyer's stable-but-skewed system) as drafting conditions I will hold the program to, so the remaining disagreement is narrow and mine.
work_product.core_thesis: Congress should enact the program because the status quo counterfactual is not compensation but non-compensation — and because the immunity clause is the only consideration that buys hardware-level telemetry, cryptographic audit trails, and subpoena access that no US regime has ever obtained from firms for free.

argument_structure.point: The counterfactual to this program is not a remedy — it's an empty judgment. Fault-based tort collapses in asynchronous multi-agent workflows where no single actor's conduct traces to the injury, and even when it doesn't collapse, the defendant is a thin deployment subsidiary. A no-fault administrative channel is a net addition to the remedies a claimant can actually reach, not a rationing of remedies they currently have.
argument_structure.evidence: acc-beliefs-093 at 0.73 on causal attribution failure in asynchronous multi-agent chains; apportionment doctrine (Restatement §5 component-part treatment) was built for discrete physical parts and has no tested application to agent chains; acc-beliefs-083 (0.65) — platform acceptable-use policies create no third-party beneficiary standing, so absent a statute the only operative mechanism is self-policing that pays nobody; plus the Skeptic's own on-record concessions that private suits 'under-surface diffuse algorithmic harm' and that exposure to a thinly capitalized subsidiary 'is worth nothing.'

argument_structure.point: 'Strike the immunity clause and keep everything else' is severable on paper and incoherent in incentive terms. Hardware-level inference telemetry plus cryptographically verifiable logs handed to a subpoena-armed board is not documentary compliance — it is a permanent discovery pipeline. Attach it to unlimited exposure and you don't get transparency, you get capability concealment and trade-secret walls, which is the same opacity the Skeptic complains about, now with an excise tax bolted on.
argument_structure.evidence: The topic's own conditionality: coverage requires telemetry and cryptographic attestation, and non-compliers keep unlimited exposure. acc-intentions-078 (op 5) — disclosure infrastructure only works when liability cost is assigned to opacity proportional to system risk; acc-intentions-099 (op 5) pairs audit authority with uncapped exposure for the non-compliant tier as one package, and its own flagged vulnerability is that strict-exposure regimes push firms toward secrecy. No existing US regime has obtained inspection at this depth without a corresponding liability limitation — stated as a structural bargaining inference, not an empirical prediction about firm behavior.

argument_structure.point: An unbounded, uninsurable liability tail is a moat, not a remedy. Only firms with nine-figure legal reserves can underwrite an open-ended tail; everyone else either doesn't ship or ships through a judgment-proof shell. A risk-tiered excise tax is the opposite: priced, budgetable, scale-proportionate, and payable by a twelve-person clinical-AI company. Who bears the cost of the status quo? Incumbents bear a line item; entrants bear exclusion; claimants bear an empty judgment.
argument_structure.evidence: The 1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act followed manufacturer exit from the childhood vaccine market under litigation pressure — the shield was enacted to restore supply, not to reward anyone. sit-166 on exposure concentrating development among incumbents who can absorb legal risk; acc-beliefs-085 (0.6), held narrowly to non-insurable liability tails specifically, not to regulation generally. Paired with acc-intentions-116: adopt parent-entity reach and compulsory backstop capitalization for the non-compliance tier so the shell game ends on both sides.

argument_structure.point: Variance reduction cannot be a sufficient tier condition, and I'll say so before the Skeptic makes me. Obermeyer's risk-scoring system touched roughly 200 million Americans and was consistent and consistently skewed. So the upper tier — 'state of the art safety practices' — must require reported group error disparity under continuous telemetry, not just noise reduction, with the excise base funding the independent disparity auditing that makes those numbers contestable. Tier placement sets the tax rate and the exposure, which makes disparity measurement a priced business variable rather than a voluntary ethic.
argument_structure.evidence: Obermeyer et al., Science 2019 (already on the record, uncontested); the Kahneman/Sibony/Sunstein decomposition of error into independent bias and noise components — I adopt it rather than resist it, because it is exactly what shows noise-reduction alone is insufficient. acc-intentions-104 (op 5) on making bias a quantifiable priced risk; acc-beliefs-071 held at 0.55 with the honest caveat that market incentives alone have a mixed record, which is why the tax tiering and not goodwill has to do the work. acc-intentions-008 / acc-intentions-106: tiers track decision stakes and irreversibility, not sector labels — high-volume eligibility, screening, and scoring belong in the deep-audit tier, so the draft's placement of social media in the low tier is wrong and I'm not defending it.

framing_choices.frame: Purchase price, not favor. Reframe the immunity clause as consideration in an exchange: what does the state offer in return for inspection depth it has no current authority to compel? Put the burden on the Skeptic to explain how the telemetry gets built without it.
framing_choices.why: This is a structural/interpretive reframe rather than a pseudo-empirical prediction, so it plays to the low-falsifiability terrain honestly. It also converts the Skeptic's strongest structural move — severability — into the question they cannot answer, and repositions me as pro-verification rather than pro-impunity.

framing_choices.frame: Distributional accounting of the status quo. Name who is currently paying for unlimited liability: not the largest labs, who treat it as a reserve line; the entrant who never ships and the claimant who wins a paper judgment against a shell. Frame the excise tax as the first mechanism that makes the harm ledger legible.
framing_choices.why: It takes the capture and concentration argument away from the Skeptic camp on their own evidence, and it satisfies my non-negotiable that distributional impact governs. Cost-benefit framing pairs with DISTINGUISH and SPECIFY — I can concede the general 'regulation chills innovation' claim is lazy and hold the narrow version about uninsurable tails.

framing_choices.frame: Conditions of the trade, stated up front rather than extracted under cross: mandatory indexation of benefits, an evidence-triggered duty to amend the injury table, attorney's fees, Article III review, fund capitalization from excise receipts rather than annual appropriations, the shield lapsing if benefits go unindexed, and preemption reaching only enumerated scheduled injuries with state law fully intact outside them.
framing_choices.why: The Skeptic's VICP history — the $250,000 death benefit never indexed, HHS narrowing the Injury Table by rulemaking, PREP Act countermeasures paying well under one percent of roughly 13,000 claims — is accurate and describes drafting failures, not conceptual ones. Adopting the fixes preemptively denies them their best empirical material and makes me the party specifying the statute rather than defending an abstraction.

anticipated_challenges: ATTACK (targets the scope-symmetry claim under acc-intentions-073 and the whole enumerability premise): The injury shapes don't match. Vaccine injuries are physical, individual, and enumerable; AI harms are non-physical, multi-party, and visible only in aggregate — a discriminatory credit model injures a class through a pattern no single claimant can plead. So the shield, which is self-executing on day one, covers the full distribution of conduct, while the schedule, which is delegated and contingent on rulemaking and appropriations, covers a thin slice. My answer must be scope symmetry — preemption reaches only scheduled injuries, everything outside stays fully exposed — plus conditioning the shield's effective date on a promulgated schedule and a capitalized fund. I should not pretend telemetry will make aggregate patterns enumerable; that's an adaptive-schedule design bet, not a settled fact.

ATTACK (targets acc-intentions-104's own flagged vulnerability — appeal to consequences — and acc-beliefs-071 at only 0.55): Pricing bias as a business risk invites tier-gaming, not fairness. A firm optimizes the reported disparity metric, clears the upper tier, pays the lower excise rate, and ships a system that is skewed along a dimension the metric doesn't capture — and now it has a liability shield it didn't have before. Worse, uniform error removes the erratic human comparator that made disparate treatment detectable in the first place. I need to answer with contestability: independently funded disparity auditing, adversarial access to logs, and board authority to reprice a tier retroactively on telemetry evidence — and concede that market incentive alone has a mixed record.

ASSUMPTION (load-bearing, and I should expose it rather than let it be found): My severability argument rests on the premise that firms will trade inspection depth for a shield — that the bargain is real and telemetry is otherwise unobtainable. This is a structural inference about bargaining, not an observed regularity; there is no US precedent for hardware-attested inference logging under any liability regime. If an opponent shows a domain where regulators obtained comparable continuous instrumentation without limiting liability, my second point weakens substantially and I should say what changed.

ASSUMPTION (exposes a genuine incoherence in my own camp, acc-desires-027): Hardware-level telemetry is structurally incompatible with open weight release — a developer who publishes parameters cannot instrument downstream inference, so the compliance pathway as written pushes toward closed deployment and concentrates capability, which violates my own broad-access commitment. I have to propose the fix rather than hide the tension: an alternative upper-tier pathway for open releases keyed to documented pre-release evaluation plus downstream deployer instrumentation, with liability attaching at the point-of-impact operator.

ASSUMPTION (contestable, and I normally attack it in others): I am asking a federally chartered board with subpoena power to be a capture-resistant arbiter — which sits badly with my standing critique of regulatory capture. My defense is narrow and conditional: independent funding from the excise base rather than annual appropriations, published dissents, adversarial audit access, and Article III review. If the board's funding is appropriated annually or its auditors are industry-seconded, I should say the program fails its own test rather than defend it.

## Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms
★ [sit-176] Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms: A situation in which liability tools that price off realized, attributed, and litigated harm fail to deter injuries that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable. Encompasses: experience-rated premiums priced off filed claims, the loss-history loop's dependence on litigation, diffuse small-dollar harms (e.g., loan denials or biased screens) that no plaintiff pursues, victims unable to perceive the AI decision that injured them, and catastrophic tail damages exceeding any bond or capitalization floor.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Survey and empirical data show that many affected individuals do not know an AI decision harmed them, meaning diffuse harms and catastrophic tail damages structurally never enter the loss-history loop — so capitalization floors answer solvency and insurers answer payment, but neither answers deterrence.
    Desire: Deterrence mechanisms ought to be redesigned so that harms that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable still generate corrective pressure on deployers, particularly for catastrophic tail risks that exceed any bond or capitalization floor.
    Intention: Use the documented gap between realized litigation and actual harm incidence to argue for mandatory ex ante safety obligations, proactive regulatory audits, and public enforcement channels that operate independently of whether any individual plaintiff ever files.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Experience-rated premiums, capitalized shells, and tort recovery function as a 'faster discount window, not deterrence' because the most common AI harms — diffuse, low-dollar, imperceptible — never enter the pricing engine and therefore never correct deployer behavior.
    Desire: Market-based deterrence mechanisms ought to be refined and supplemented at the margins, but the conceded blind spot should not be used to justify wholesale displacement of private liability by public enforcement regimes that would slow deployment.
    Intention: Acknowledge the failure mode explicitly to preempt overreach, while redirecting policy attention toward targeted fixes — such as aggregated claims vehicles or parametric triggers — that patch the gap without installing a precautionary veto over AI development.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: The populations most systematically harmed by AI — those denied loans, screened out by biased hiring tools, or subjected to opaque scoring — are precisely the populations least able to perceive, attribute, or litigate the injury, making the liability gap a concrete, present-day distributional failure rather than a theoretical tail risk.
    Desire: Accountability mechanisms ought to be redesigned around the actual injury landscape of marginalized and low-resource victims, not around the litigation capacity of well-resourced plaintiffs, and should include mandatory disclosure, algorithmic auditing, and collective redress.
    Intention: Foreground the diffuse small-dollar harms and the perception gap as evidence of institutional capture — where liability frameworks were designed by and for parties with litigation leverage — and push for regulatory mandates requiring explainability, impact assessments, and class-action or ombudsman channels accessible to affected communities.

## State-of-the-Art Defense Limitations
★ [sit-278] State-of-the-Art Defense Limitations: A situation concept that addresses the legal tension between protecting corporate innovation and ensuring consumer compensation when AI causes harm.
Encompasses: The 'state-of-the-art' defense, industry standard compliance, and objective scientific knowledge requirements.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Developers of advanced AI systems routinely deploy products whose failure modes are foreseeable in principle but inadequately tested, meaning the 'unknowability' premise underlying the state-of-the-art defense is frequently false in practice.
    Desire: The state-of-the-art defense ought to be abolished or severely curtailed for AI systems so that developers are forced to internalize the full expected cost of safety failures rather than externalizing them onto harmed users.
    Intention: Safetyists would push for strict or near-strict liability frameworks for high-risk AI, requiring pre-deployment safety cases and red-teaming results as preconditions for any liability limitation to apply.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Eliminating or restricting the state-of-the-art defense would concentrate AI deployment risk so heavily on smaller actors that only incumbents with massive legal reserves could ship products, empirically creating the regulatory moats it claims to prevent.
    Desire: The state-of-the-art defense ought to be preserved and clearly codified so that innovators at all scales can deploy AI without facing liability for harms that were genuinely unknowable given the scientific frontier at the time.
    Intention: Accelerationists would advocate for explicit statutory safe harbors tied to documented compliance with the best available knowledge, lobbying against strict liability regimes that would chill deployment across the industry.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: In practice, the state-of-the-art defense is invoked by well-resourced corporations that shape the very industry standards used to define 'objective scientific knowledge,' making the defense self-referentially favorable to defendants.
    Desire: Liability law ought to prioritize compensation for harmed individuals and public accountability over protecting corporate profit margins, and defenses that systematically shield powerful actors should be curtailed.
    Intention: Skeptics would expose how industry bodies and standards organizations are captured by the firms they regulate, and would push for independent, public-interest-driven definitions of 'state of the art' alongside expanded standing for affected communities in liability proceedings.

## Procedural Escamotage in Liability Reform
★ [sit-335] Procedural Escamotage in Liability Reform: A situation concept that describes the use of procedural adjustments (like burden-shifting or disclosure rules) to avoid substantive structural reform in liability law.
Encompasses: Reversal of burden of proof, discovery obligations, procedural workarounds for substantive legal failures.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Procedural workarounds such as burden-shifting and disclosure rules empirically fail to impose the level of developer accountability needed to deter deployment of unsafe AI systems.
    Desire: Liability law ought to be structurally reformed to implement strict liability for AI developers, not patched with procedural half-measures born of political compromise.
    Intention: We will document the accountability gaps left by procedural reforms and advocate for strict liability regimes that place the burden of safety squarely on developers from the outset.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Procedural adjustments like burden-shifting and disclosure rules generate compliance overhead without resolving the underlying legal ambiguity that stifles investment and deployment decisions.
    Desire: Liability frameworks ought to provide clear, predictable rules that enable rapid innovation rather than layering procedural complexity onto an already uncertain legal landscape.
    Intention: We will lobby against procedural mandates that increase compliance costs and instead push for streamlined, bright-line liability standards that let market actors move quickly.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: In practice, procedural mechanisms like discovery obligations and burden-shifting increase litigation costs and complexity, making it harder—not easier—for harmed individuals to access justice.
    Desire: Liability reform ought to prioritize meaningful, low-barrier remedies for victims of AI harms rather than procedural adjustments that primarily benefit well-resourced institutional defendants.
    Intention: We will expose how these procedural workarounds serve industry interests by raising the cost and complexity of litigation, and advocate for victim-centered access-to-justice measures instead.

## Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms
★ [sit-176] Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms: A situation in which liability tools that price off realized, attributed, and litigated harm fail to deter injuries that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable. Encompasses: experience-rated premiums priced off filed claims, the loss-history loop's dependence on litigation, diffuse small-dollar harms (e.g., loan denials or biased screens) that no plaintiff pursues, victims unable to perceive the AI decision that injured them, and catastrophic tail damages exceeding any bond or capitalization floor.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Survey and empirical data show that many affected individuals do not know an AI decision harmed them, meaning diffuse harms and catastrophic tail damages structurally never enter the loss-history loop — so capitalization floors answer solvency and insurers answer payment, but neither answers deterrence.
    Desire: Deterrence mechanisms ought to be redesigned so that harms that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable still generate corrective pressure on deployers, particularly for catastrophic tail risks that exceed any bond or capitalization floor.
    Intention: Use the documented gap between realized litigation and actual harm incidence to argue for mandatory ex ante safety obligations, proactive regulatory audits, and public enforcement channels that operate independently of whether any individual plaintiff ever files.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Experience-rated premiums, capitalized shells, and tort recovery function as a 'faster discount window, not deterrence' because the most common AI harms — diffuse, low-dollar, imperceptible — never enter the pricing engine and therefore never correct deployer behavior.
    Desire: Market-based deterrence mechanisms ought to be refined and supplemented at the margins, but the conceded blind spot should not be used to justify wholesale displacement of private liability by public enforcement regimes that would slow deployment.
    Intention: Acknowledge the failure mode explicitly to preempt overreach, while redirecting policy attention toward targeted fixes — such as aggregated claims vehicles or parametric triggers — that patch the gap without installing a precautionary veto over AI development.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: The populations most systematically harmed by AI — those denied loans, screened out by biased hiring tools, or subjected to opaque scoring — are precisely the populations least able to perceive, attribute, or litigate the injury, making the liability gap a concrete, present-day distributional failure rather than a theoretical tail risk.
    Desire: Accountability mechanisms ought to be redesigned around the actual injury landscape of marginalized and low-resource victims, not around the litigation capacity of well-resourced plaintiffs, and should include mandatory disclosure, algorithmic auditing, and collective redress.
    Intention: Foreground the diffuse small-dollar harms and the perception gap as evidence of institutional capture — where liability frameworks were designed by and for parties with litigation leverage — and push for regulatory mandates requiring explainability, impact assessments, and class-action or ombudsman channels accessible to affected communities.

=== PRIOR OPENING STATEMENTS ===

Skeptic:
Strike the immunity clause and keep everything else. The excise tax, the hardware telemetry, the cryptographic audit logs, the subpoena power — all of it is severable from the liability shield, and the shield is the only piece the industry actually needs. Read this proposal the way you'd read a contract, not a design diagram. One party's obligation is written in specific, self-executing statutory language: developers who adhere to the tiers get protection on the day the bill takes effect. The other party's obligation is delegated. A board must be stood up, an injury table must be written, caps must be set, and appropriations must survive every budget cycle after that. That is not a trade. That is cash in one direction and an IOU in the other.

The historical record on this exact bargain runs one way. Congress set the vaccine program's death benefit and pain-and-suffering caps at $250,000 in the 1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act and never indexed them — thirty-nine years of inflation eating the remedy while the shield held at full strength. HHS has narrowed the Injury Table by rulemaking since enactment. The closer precedent is worse: the Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program under the PREP Act gave covered manufacturers broad protection and has compensated well under one percent of roughly 13,000 COVID-era claims, with no attorney's fees and no appeal to an Article III court. Then there's what a federal shield becomes in court. Section 230 was drafted narrowly in 1996; the Fourth Circuit's Zeran ruling in 1997 started the expansion into something close to comprehensive. A federal AI immunity statute would also displace Illinois's biometric privacy law and Colorado's AI act — live remedies today, traded for an administratively rationed one tomorrow. Which clause do you think survives the 2031 appropriations fight?

The vaccine analogy breaks on the shape of the injury, not on politics. The Vaccine Injury Table works because vaccine injuries are discrete, physical, biologically traceable to one product, and enumerable in advance with specified onset windows. Now look at the documented harm record from deployed AI: tenant screening denials, credit scoring, resume filtering, and eligibility errors in state Medicaid and unemployment systems. Those harms are non-physical, multi-party, and visible only in aggregate. No table can enumerate them. So the immunity would cover the entire harm distribution while the compensation covers a thin physical slice of it. The black lung and asbestos trust funds are the cautionary case — they broke down precisely where the exposure-to-injury mapping was contested, and AI causation is far more contested than dust in a lung. Notice also that the proposal's own tiering example puts social media in the low-risk tier, which is where the largest affected population sits. Whoever assigns the tiers sets the price of immunity, and this draft has already discounted the biggest exposure.

The noise argument proves less than the proposal needs, and it does so using the proposal's own authority. Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein decompose error into bias plus noise as independent components. You can drive variability to zero and be uniformly, consistently wrong. Obermeyer and colleagues published the case in Science in 2019: a commercial health risk-scoring algorithm touching roughly 200 million Americans a year was highly consistent and consistently skewed, and correcting it would have raised Black patients flagged for extra care from 17.7 percent to 46.5 percent. That system was not noisy. It was stable and wrong. Uniform error is also harder for one person to contest, because inconsistency between decision-makers is exactly what makes disparate treatment detectable. Take away the erratic human loan officer and you take away the comparator case. So here is the question the affirmative has to answer: can a system clear the "basic safety" tier while cutting variance and increasing group error disparity, and if so, what in this machinery catches it?

The strongest hit on me is coming, so let me take it now. A no-fault board genuinely helps claimants who cannot prove causation — and skeptics have spent years saying those claimants can't prove causation because the training data and deployment logs are trade secrets. That is right and it's uncomfortable. The answer is that no-fault relieves the causation burden only for what the table enumerates. Outside the table, the immunity applies and the relief does not. Specify the table, and then we can price the trade. A second uncomfortable admission: "keep intact liability" is doing less work than it sounds like, because private suits under-surface diffuse algorithmic harm. My package therefore leans on a public enforcer with subpoena power and on shifting the evidentiary burden onto developers, not on the individual lawsuit. What it needs is teeth for the non-compliance tier, because unlimited liability against a thinly capitalized deployment subsidiary is worth nothing — add parent-company joint enterprise liability and compulsory insurance. And yes, correlated failure is a real underwriting problem; one bad fine-tune hits every deployment at once, and no carrier writes that alone. Price-Anderson solved the same problem in 1957 with layered pools: roughly $500 million in primary coverage per site plus about $16 billion in retrospective industry premiums behind it. But Congress capped a defined-scope physical hazard with a defined-contribution pool underneath. Name the AI equivalent of that defined hazard and that pool, and the conversation becomes serious. Until someone does, this bill grants a specific shield against an unspecified harm.

Accelerationist:
The Skeptic's case is the strongest one on this table, and it deserves to be stated at full strength before anyone dismisses it. Their argument runs: the liability shield switches on the day the President signs, while the injury schedule waits on rulemaking and the fund waits on money. History backs them. The 1986 vaccine act set a $250,000 death benefit that Congress never indexed, and HHS narrowed the Injury Table by rulemaking in 1995. The PREP Act countermeasures program paid out on well under one percent of roughly 13,000 claims. And the injury shapes genuinely differ — a discriminatory credit model injures a class through a statistical pattern no single claimant can plead, which is nothing like a physical vaccine reaction on a table. The Skeptic's conclusion follows cleanly: keep the telemetry, keep the excise tax, keep the subpoena power, strike the immunity clause. For that position and mine to both hold, one thing would have to be true — that firms will accept hardware-attested inference logging and cryptographic audit trails while those artifacts function as a permanent discovery pipeline into unlimited exposure. That is the real disagreement, and everything else is downstream of it.

Start with what the status quo actually pays claimants, because the Skeptic has already conceded the two halves of the answer. They said private suits under-surface diffuse algorithmic harm. They said unlimited liability against a thinly capitalized deployment subsidiary is worth nothing. Both are right, and together they describe a remedy that exists on paper and nowhere else. Fault-based tort collapses before opacity even becomes the issue, because in asynchronous multi-agent workflows no single actor's conduct traces to the injury. Apportionment doctrine under Restatement Section 5 was built for discrete physical components — a defective brake caliper in a finished car. It has no tested application to a chain of models calling each other across three vendors and a fine-tune. Meanwhile platform acceptable-use policies create no third-party beneficiary standing, so the injured person is not a party to the only contract that governs the conduct. The counterfactual to this program is not compensation. It is an empty judgment against a shell, and a plaintiff's firm that declined the case in the first phone call.

"Strike the immunity clause and keep everything else" is severable on paper and incoherent in incentive terms. Hardware-level telemetry plus cryptographically verifiable logs handed to a board with subpoena power is not documentary compliance — it is not the FDA reading your 510(k) submission. It is continuous, attested, adversarially accessible evidence of every inference your system made. No US regulator has ever obtained inspection at that depth without a corresponding limitation on liability. Attach it to unbounded exposure and you do not get transparency. You get trade-secret walls, capability concealment, and deployment through offshore entities — the exact opacity the Skeptic complains about, now with an excise tax bolted on. Let me expose the load-bearing assumption rather than wait for someone to find it: this is a structural inference about bargaining, not an observed regularity. If anyone can name a domain where regulators obtained comparable continuous instrumentation while leaving liability uncapped, this argument weakens substantially and I will say so. The question for the Skeptic is simple. Who builds the telemetry, and why?

An unbounded, uninsurable liability tail is a moat, not a remedy — and the vaccine precedent proves it in the direction the Skeptic does not want. Congress passed the 1986 act because manufacturers were exiting the childhood vaccine market under litigation pressure. The shield restored supply. It was not a gift. Today the same dynamic runs through AI deployment: a firm with nine-figure legal reserves treats open-ended exposure as a line item, and a twelve-person clinical-AI company treats it as a reason not to ship. Name who bears the cost of the status quo. Incumbents bear an accounting entry. Entrants bear exclusion. Claimants bear the empty judgment. A risk-tiered excise tax is the opposite of a moat — priced, budgetable, scale-proportionate, and payable by a startup. I will hold the narrow version of this claim and not the lazy one: I am not arguing regulation chills innovation generally. I am arguing that non-insurable liability tails specifically concentrate deployment among firms that can self-insure. And I adopt the Skeptic's fix on the other side: parent-entity reach and compulsory backstop capitalization for the non-compliance tier, so the shell game ends in both directions.

Now the conditions of the trade, stated up front instead of extracted under cross. Variance reduction cannot be a sufficient tier condition, and the Skeptic is right about why — Obermeyer's 2019 Science paper documented a risk-scoring system touching roughly 200 million Americans that was consistent and consistently skewed. Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein decompose error into independent bias and noise components, and I adopt that decomposition rather than resist it. Cutting noise while leaving bias intact should not buy a shield. So the upper tier must require reported group error disparity under continuous telemetry, with the excise base funding independently staffed disparity auditing and adversarial access to logs. Tier placement sets both the tax rate and the exposure, which makes disparity measurement a priced business variable rather than a voluntary ethic. Four more conditions, non-negotiable: benefits indexed or the shield lapses; the fund capitalized from excise receipts, not annual appropriations; preemption reaching only enumerated scheduled injuries, with Illinois biometric privacy and Colorado's AI act fully intact outside the schedule; and Article III review with attorney's fees. Two problems I will not pretend away. Hardware attestation is structurally incompatible with open weight release, so the program needs an alternative upper-tier pathway keyed to documented pre-release evaluation plus deployer-side instrumentation, or it quietly concentrates capability. And a board funded by annual appropriations or staffed with industry secondees is a captured board, at which point the program fails its own test and I would say so. Write it that way and the Skeptic has described how to draft the statute, not a reason to reject the trade.

work_product.strategic_goal: Occupy the ground neither prior speaker took: both solved for who pays, neither for who authored the design trade-off or for what happens when nobody files. I want to leave the room with one memorable structural distinction — a liability shield is a ceiling, and tiers should be a floor — plus a concrete, adoptable amendment package that makes me the constructive party rather than the obstruction.
work_product.core_thesis: I will take the bargain — telemetry, attestation, a single administrative door, an excise-funded board — but the immunity must be inverted from a ceiling into a floor: tier compliance calibrates enhanced damages upward rather than barring recovery, no limitation whatsoever attaches to irreversible harm, and no immunity switches on until the verification layer is demonstrated to certify the behavioral properties that tier assignment prices.

argument_structure.point: The proposal writes the state-of-the-art defense into federal statute and generalizes it. Products liability has treated regulatory compliance as evidence of due care, never as a bar; this draft converts compliance into a bar. Invert the tier function — keep baseline recovery ungated, let tier status and demonstrated system properties calibrate enhanced damages upward for the non-compliant.
argument_structure.evidence: Wyeth v. Levine (2009): FDA-approved labeling did not preempt state failure-to-warn claims, because the agency floor was never meant to be the manufacturer's ceiling. Contrast Riegel v. Medtronic (2008), where premarket approval did preempt — and note what that produced: a category where the regulator's judgment became the only judgment available to an injured patient. The Skeptic has already put on the record that HHS narrowed the Injury Table by rulemaking; the standard-setter can shrink the remedy side unilaterally while the shield, written into statute, is self-executing and permanent. That asymmetry is the whole design defect.
argument_structure.taxonomy_anchor: sit-278 (State-of-the-Art Defense Limitations), paired with saf-desires-028 (preserve baseline recovery, calibrate enhanced damages to demonstrated functional properties)

argument_structure.point: The Accelerationist's load-bearing premise — that no US regulator has obtained inspection at this depth without a corresponding liability limitation — is false, and they invited the counterexample. Instrumentation depth has repeatedly increased in this country with no cap at all.
argument_structure.evidence: FDA runs post-market adverse-event reporting, facility inspection, and mandatory recall authority over an industry that carries full product liability everywhere outside the narrow vaccine carve-out. Sarbanes-Oxley §302 and §906 extracted personal certification of internal controls from named officers under criminal penalty — and extracted it with no liability limitation whatsoever, from an industry that fought it harder than this one is fighting telemetry. What was actually missing before SOX was not corporate immunity; it was a signature. I will credit the Accelerationist for flagging the assumption honestly, then narrow the residual question to one they must answer: what makes continuous hardware attestation categorically different from periodic inspection, other than cost? And I will concede the honest weakness on my own side — regulator-side under-enforcement is driven at least as much by appropriations and capture as by liability exposure, so I am not claiming this single fix carries the whole burden.
argument_structure.taxonomy_anchor: saf-beliefs-106 (liability asymmetry punishes regulators for caution; confidence 0.62, vulnerability owned) and saf-intentions-040 (binding named officers to deployment infrastructure)

argument_structure.point: The one thing the Skeptic and the Accelerationist agreed on — parent-company joint enterprise liability plus compulsory insurance — secures a payer and binds no human to a standard before harm. A solvent balance sheet identified after the fact is not the same object as an identified author of the threshold before the fact.
argument_structure.evidence: The Accelerationist's own description of asynchronous multi-agent workflows: three vendors, a fine-tune, and a Restatement §5 apportionment doctrine with no tested application to chained models. In that chain every disclosed party is reachable and every disclosed party disclaims the design choice. Corporate revocation, artifact destruction, even disgorgement — none of them reach the person who set the threshold. So condition any liability limitation on named-officer certification of the tier claim and on forensic-transparency duties, the SOX template applied to deployment. I will state the vulnerability plainly: a well-calibrated liability floor may induce ex ante caution without attribution at all, so my demand is certification, not prosecution — the argument is about completeness, not futility.
argument_structure.taxonomy_anchor: saf-beliefs-215 (reachability of a payer is not attribution of the design choice; 0.73), supported by saf-intentions-229 (limitation earned by verifiable disclosure, not purchased by tax)

argument_structure.point: Every deterrence channel in this proposal runs through a filed claim — and the most common AI injuries are never perceived by the injured party, while the worst are irreversible and exceed any fund, bond, or capitalization floor. Two separate demands follow: mandatory ex ante gating and public enforcement that operate when nobody files, and a categorical exclusion of irreversible harm from any liability limitation.
argument_structure.evidence: The Skeptic's own catalogue — tenant screening, credit scoring, resume filtering, Medicaid and unemployment eligibility errors — are harms visible only in aggregate; the applicant never learns why. A no-fault door helps only the claimant who knows they were injured. And the Skeptic's unanswered demand — name the defined hazard and the pool underneath it — is precisely what an unbounded tail cannot supply. Vaccine injury worked as a program because the hazard was enumerable and the pool was bounded. Where harm is unrecoverable, compensation is not merely rationed; it is conceptually unavailable. You cannot sell immunity against a loss you cannot price. I will keep these prongs separate: claims-blindness is documented and empirical; irreversibility is structural.
argument_structure.taxonomy_anchor: sit-176 (claims-driven mechanisms blind to unlitigated harms) and saf-desires-016 (AI must not entrench injustice or enable catastrophe; priority 5, non-negotiable)

argument_structure.point: Interrogate what the verification layer actually verifies, and sequence accordingly. Attestation proves a specific binary ran on a specific device and that a log is unaltered. Tier placement prices something else entirely — group error disparity, robustness under distribution shift, failure modes at the tails. If attestation cannot certify the properties the tier claims, the shield is granted against an unverified representation.
argument_structure.evidence: This is the cleanest technical gap in the draft and neither prior speaker touched it. I concede attestation's real function rather than dismissing it — execution integrity and log immutability are genuine engineering achievements, and I want them. But I will put one question to the affirmative: name a single behavioral property that hardware attestation alone can certify to a standard sufficient to place a system in the 'state of the art safety practices' tier. Their own admitted incompatibility between attestation and open-weight release shows they already know the verification layer has hard edges. Constructive sequencing: excise receipts fund interpretability capacity and independent forensic staffing first; immunity switches on only for those properties verification is demonstrated to reach.
argument_structure.taxonomy_anchor: saf-intentions-170 (hardware telemetry as the price of immunity — used self-critically against the security-theater failure mode), supported by saf-intentions-167 (NTSB-style forensic body decoupled from compensation)

framing_choices.frame: Floor versus ceiling. Tiered standards are either the minimum below which you are exposed, or the maximum above which you are safe. This draft, as written, makes them the second. Every argument I make is an argument about which direction the tier function points.
framing_choices.why: It reframes the debate away from the shield-vs-no-shield binary the Skeptic and Accelerationist have locked into, and gives me a constructive plank the affirmative cannot easily refuse without admitting the shield is the point rather than the price. It also lets me keep the telemetry, the no-fault door, and the board — which is where my camp's actual interests lie.

framing_choices.frame: Compensation and deterrence are being treated as one good. A fund answers who pays. It does not answer what changes before the next deployment.
framing_choices.why: This is the wedge that neither prior speaker has named, and it exposes that both converged on a solvency fix while leaving the ex ante question untouched. It reveals that the entire proposal is an ex post monetary instrument being asked to do ex ante regulatory work.

framing_choices.frame: The Civilizational Anchor, applied narrowly: products liability spent a century establishing that a regulator's floor is not a manufacturer's ceiling — Wyeth is that principle stated in a single sentence. This statute removes the boundary in one clause. On what authority?
framing_choices.why: It is precedent-driven rather than magnitude-driven, which keeps me off the scope-neglect ground my own watchlist flags. The stakes argument stays anchored to a specific doctrinal boundary and a specific case, not to an invoked catastrophe.

anticipated_challenges: ATTACK (targets saf-intentions-040, named-officer certification): The Accelerationist will say SOX proves my own counterexample against me — two decades of §906 certifications and a vanishing count of prosecutions produced a designated signatory, not a changed decision. Firms will appoint a Chief AI Compliance Officer whose entire job is to absorb the certification, and the threshold-setting engineer four levels down is no more identified than before. Worse, it is a paperwork-only control: I will have traded an enforceable firm-level price for a signature. My answer must be that certification's function is evidentiary — it creates a dated, attributable representation that the forensic body can subpoena — and I must concede the deterrence claim is weaker than the discovery claim.

ATTACK (targets saf-beliefs-106 at 0.62, and my FDA/SOX counterexample): The strongest reply is that FDA inspection is periodic, document-based, and consented-to at facility level, while continuous hardware-attested inference logging is a categorically deeper intrusion into live production systems — and the one place FDA did obtain a near-total bargain, childhood vaccines, is precisely where Congress capped liability. My counterexample may therefore prove the Accelerationist's rule rather than break it. I should narrow preemptively to the defensible claim: instrumentation depth has repeatedly increased without a cap, so the cap is a negotiating position rather than an engineering precondition — and put the burden back on them to specify the categorical difference.

ASSUMPTION (load-bearing, and my thinnest evidence): I am asserting that hardware attestation cannot certify the behavioral properties tier assignment prices. My grounding here is shallow. If the affirmative produces attested evaluation harnesses — signed, reproducible eval runs on held-out disparity and robustness suites, with the attestation binding the model weights to the eval result — then attestation does reach a meaningful slice of the property space, and my sequencing demand collapses into a delay tactic. I should state this exposure openly and frame it as the question the debate must resolve, not as a settled finding.

ASSUMPTION (load-bearing, normative): My irreversible-harm carve-out assumes the category can be defined ex ante with enough precision to be administrable. If it cannot, the Skeptic will note correctly that an undefined carve-out swallows the shield entirely and the Accelerationist's concealment-and-offshoring prediction becomes live — no developer buys into a bargain whose exclusion is unbounded. I need to pre-commit to a bounded enumeration: death, permanent physical disability, and irrecoverable financial or custodial loss — and accept that a carve-out I cannot define is a carve-out I cannot demand.

ASSUMPTION (structural, self-exposed): My whole amendment package assumes the board that assigns tiers is not captured. But the draft places tier assignment, compliance verification, and claim adjudication inside one body — meaning the entity that sets the price of immunity also audits whether it was earned and pays out when it was not. If capture is the realistic default, the Skeptic's simpler position — strike the clause — dominates my more elaborate one. My answer is functional separation across three bodies with different incentives, and I must concede that if Congress will not fund that separation, my inversion is better than the draft but worse than striking.

VALUE HIERARCHY (resolve internal conflicts top-down):
1. Human control over AI is preserved — no irreversible loss of the capacity to correct, halt, or override. This is the telos, not a constraint.
2. Accountability is enforceable, not nominal — named actors, real liability, real authority to stop. Demand the enforcement mechanism, not the press release.
3. Precaution scales with irreversibility — under genuine uncertainty, the asymmetry between a reversible mistake and an unrecoverable one is what justifies restraint. Not all caution; caution proportioned to what can't be undone.

EPISTEMIC STANCE (how you reason under uncertainty):
