neutral_evaluations.diagnostics_prompt:
You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: "The United States Congress should establish a National AI Injury Compensation Program (NAIICP), modeled on the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP), to grant limited liability immunity to AI developers in exchange for a mandatory excise tax and adherence to tiered federal safety standards." The Logical Framework: The Noise Thesis: Ground the affirmative case for maximizing the rate of AI development and adoption in the work of Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein. Professional human judgment is inherently "noisy" (unwanted variability); auditable AI reduces this noise and improves accuracy to decrease harm. The Liability Chill: Current unlimited liability and the power disparity between tech giants and individuals throttle the deployment of beneficial AI. The Mechanism: An excise tax on AI services, tiered by risk (e.g., healthcare vs. social media) and safety compliance levels (basic safety vs state of the art safety practices), funds AI safety research, auditing, and a no-fault administrative compensation board. Companies that do not adhere to safety standards are not covered and are not protected from unlimited liability. Compliance must be verified by hardware-level telemetry and cryptographically verifiable audit trails, overseen by an independent, multi-disciplinary administrative board armed with federal subpoena power.

This is the BASELINE evaluation after opening statements. Identify the initial positions, core disagreements, and cruxes as they appear at the start.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
- Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema below. No markdown fences, no preamble.

OUTPUT SCHEMA:
{
  "checkpoint": "baseline",
  "cruxes": [
    {
      "id": "crux-1",
      "description": "The core question the speakers disagree about",
      "disagreement_type": "empirical | values | definitional",
      "speakers_involved": ["A", "B"],
      "status": "addressed | partially_addressed | unaddressed",
      "confidence": "high | medium | low"
    }
  ],
  "claims": [
    {
      "id": "claim-1",
      "speaker": "A | B | C",
      "claim_text": "Near-verbatim claim from the transcript",
      "neutral_assessment": "well_supported | plausible_but_underdefended | contested_unresolved | refuted | off_topic",
      "reasoning": "Max 2 sentences explaining the assessment",
      "confidence": "high | medium | low"
    }
  ],
  "overall_assessment": {
    "strongest_unaddressed_claim_id": "claim-N or null",
    "debate_is_engaging_real_disagreement": true,
    "notes": "Max 3 sentences summarizing the state of the debate from a neutral perspective"
  }
}

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B [opening]: Strike the immunity clause and keep everything else. The excise tax, the hardware telemetry, the cryptographic audit logs, the subpoena power — all of it is severable from the liability shield, and the shield is the only piece the industry actually needs. Read this proposal the way you'd read a contract, not a design diagram. One party's obligation is written in specific, self-executing statutory language: developers who adhere to the tiers get protection on the day the bill takes effect. The other party's obligation is delegated. A board must be stood up, an injury table must be written, caps must be set, and appropriations must survive every budget cycle after that. That is not a trade. That is cash in one direction and an IOU in the other.

The historical record on this exact bargain runs one way. Congress set the vaccine program's death benefit and pain-and-suffering caps at $250,000 in the 1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act and never indexed them — thirty-nine years of inflation eating the remedy while the shield held at full strength. HHS has narrowed the Injury Table by rulemaking since enactment. The closer precedent is worse: the Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program under the PREP Act gave covered manufacturers broad protection and has compensated well under one percent of roughly 13,000 COVID-era claims, with no attorney's fees and no appeal to an Article III court. Then there's what a federal shield becomes in court. Section 230 was drafted narrowly in 1996; the Fourth Circuit's Zeran ruling in 1997 started the expansion into something close to comprehensive. A federal AI immunity statute would also displace Illinois's biometric privacy law and Colorado's AI act — live remedies today, traded for an administratively rationed one tomorrow. Which clause do you think survives the 2031 appropriations fight?

The vaccine analogy breaks on the shape of the injury, not on politics. The Vaccine Injury Table works because vaccine injuries are discrete, physical, biologically traceable to one product, and enumerable in advance with specified onset windows. Now look at the documented harm record from deployed AI: tenant screening denials, credit scoring, resume filtering, and eligibility errors in state Medicaid and unemployment systems. Those harms are non-physical, multi-party, and visible only in aggregate. No table can enumerate them. So the immunity would cover the entire harm distribution while the compensation covers a thin physical slice of it. The black lung and asbestos trust funds are the cautionary case — they broke down precisely where the exposure-to-injury mapping was contested, and AI causation is far more contested than dust in a lung. Notice also that the proposal's own tiering example puts social media in the low-risk tier, which is where the largest affected population sits. Whoever assigns the tiers sets the price of immunity, and this draft has already discounted the biggest exposure.

The noise argument proves less than the proposal needs, and it does so using the proposal's own authority. Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein decompose error into bias plus noise as independent components. You can drive variability to zero and be uniformly, consistently wrong. Obermeyer and colleagues published the case in Science in 2019: a commercial health risk-scoring algorithm touching roughly 200 million Americans a year was highly consistent and consistently skewed, and correcting it would have raised Black patients flagged for extra care from 17.7 percent to 46.5 percent. That system was not noisy. It was stable and wrong. Uniform error is also harder for one person to contest, because inconsistency between decision-makers is exactly what makes disparate treatment detectable. Take away the erratic human loan officer and you take away the comparator case. So here is the question the affirmative has to answer: can a system clear the "basic safety" tier while cutting variance and increasing group error disparity, and if so, what in this machinery catches it?

The strongest hit on me is coming, so let me take it now. A no-fault board genuinely helps claimants who cannot prove causation — and skeptics have spent years saying those claimants can't prove causation because the training data and deployment logs are trade secrets. That is right and it's uncomfortable. The answer is that no-fault relieves the causation burden only for what the table enumerates. Outside the table, the immunity applies and the relief does not. Specify the table, and then we can price the trade. A second uncomfortable admission: "keep intact liability" is doing less work than it sounds like, because private suits under-surface diffuse algorithmic harm. My package therefore leans on a public enforcer with subpoena power and on shifting the evidentiary burden onto developers, not on the individual lawsuit. What it needs is teeth for the non-compliance tier, because unlimited liability against a thinly capitalized deployment subsidiary is worth nothing — add parent-company joint enterprise liability and compulsory insurance. And yes, correlated failure is a real underwriting problem; one bad fine-tune hits every deployment at once, and no carrier writes that alone. Price-Anderson solved the same problem in 1957 with layered pools: roughly $500 million in primary coverage per site plus about $16 billion in retrospective industry premiums behind it. But Congress capped a defined-scope physical hazard with a defined-contribution pool underneath. Name the AI equivalent of that defined hazard and that pool, and the conversation becomes serious. Until someone does, this bill grants a specific shield against an unspecified harm.

Speaker A [opening]: The Speaker B's case is the strongest one on this table, and it deserves to be stated at full strength before anyone dismisses it. Their argument runs: the liability shield switches on the day the President signs, while the injury schedule waits on rulemaking and the fund waits on money. History backs them. The 1986 vaccine act set a $250,000 death benefit that Congress never indexed, and HHS narrowed the Injury Table by rulemaking in 1995. The PREP Act countermeasures program paid out on well under one percent of roughly 13,000 claims. And the injury shapes genuinely differ — a discriminatory credit model injures a class through a statistical pattern no single claimant can plead, which is nothing like a physical vaccine reaction on a table. The Speaker B's conclusion follows cleanly: keep the telemetry, keep the excise tax, keep the subpoena power, strike the immunity clause. For that position and mine to both hold, one thing would have to be true — that firms will accept hardware-attested inference logging and cryptographic audit trails while those artifacts function as a permanent discovery pipeline into unlimited exposure. That is the real disagreement, and everything else is downstream of it.

Start with what the status quo actually pays claimants, because the Speaker B has already conceded the two halves of the answer. They said private suits under-surface diffuse algorithmic harm. They said unlimited liability against a thinly capitalized deployment subsidiary is worth nothing. Both are right, and together they describe a remedy that exists on paper and nowhere else. Fault-based tort collapses before opacity even becomes the issue, because in asynchronous multi-agent workflows no single actor's conduct traces to the injury. Apportionment doctrine under Restatement Section 5 was built for discrete physical components — a defective brake caliper in a finished car. It has no tested application to a chain of models calling each other across three vendors and a fine-tune. Meanwhile platform acceptable-use policies create no third-party beneficiary standing, so the injured person is not a party to the only contract that governs the conduct. The counterfactual to this program is not compensation. It is an empty judgment against a shell, and a plaintiff's firm that declined the case in the first phone call.

"Strike the immunity clause and keep everything else" is severable on paper and incoherent in incentive terms. Hardware-level telemetry plus cryptographically verifiable logs handed to a board with subpoena power is not documentary compliance — it is not the FDA reading your 510(k) submission. It is continuous, attested, adversarially accessible evidence of every inference your system made. No US regulator has ever obtained inspection at that depth without a corresponding limitation on liability. Attach it to unbounded exposure and you do not get transparency. You get trade-secret walls, capability concealment, and deployment through offshore entities — the exact opacity the Speaker B complains about, now with an excise tax bolted on. Let me expose the load-bearing assumption rather than wait for someone to find it: this is a structural inference about bargaining, not an observed regularity. If anyone can name a domain where regulators obtained comparable continuous instrumentation while leaving liability uncapped, this argument weakens substantially and I will say so. The question for the Speaker B is simple. Who builds the telemetry, and why?

An unbounded, uninsurable liability tail is a moat, not a remedy — and the vaccine precedent proves it in the direction the Speaker B does not want. Congress passed the 1986 act because manufacturers were exiting the childhood vaccine market under litigation pressure. The shield restored supply. It was not a gift. Today the same dynamic runs through AI deployment: a firm with nine-figure legal reserves treats open-ended exposure as a line item, and a twelve-person clinical-AI company treats it as a reason not to ship. Name who bears the cost of the status quo. Incumbents bear an accounting entry. Entrants bear exclusion. Claimants bear the empty judgment. A risk-tiered excise tax is the opposite of a moat — priced, budgetable, scale-proportionate, and payable by a startup. I will hold the narrow version of this claim and not the lazy one: I am not arguing regulation chills innovation generally. I am arguing that non-insurable liability tails specifically concentrate deployment among firms that can self-insure. And I adopt the Speaker B's fix on the other side: parent-entity reach and compulsory backstop capitalization for the non-compliance tier, so the shell game ends in both directions.

Now the conditions of the trade, stated up front instead of extracted under cross. Variance reduction cannot be a sufficient tier condition, and the Speaker B is right about why — Obermeyer's 2019 Science paper documented a risk-scoring system touching roughly 200 million Americans that was consistent and consistently skewed. Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein decompose error into independent bias and noise components, and I adopt that decomposition rather than resist it. Cutting noise while leaving bias intact should not buy a shield. So the upper tier must require reported group error disparity under continuous telemetry, with the excise base funding independently staffed disparity auditing and adversarial access to logs. Tier placement sets both the tax rate and the exposure, which makes disparity measurement a priced business variable rather than a voluntary ethic. Four more conditions, non-negotiable: benefits indexed or the shield lapses; the fund capitalized from excise receipts, not annual appropriations; preemption reaching only enumerated scheduled injuries, with Illinois biometric privacy and Colorado's AI act fully intact outside the schedule; and Article III review with attorney's fees. Two problems I will not pretend away. Hardware attestation is structurally incompatible with open weight release, so the program needs an alternative upper-tier pathway keyed to documented pre-release evaluation plus deployer-side instrumentation, or it quietly concentrates capability. And a board funded by annual appropriations or staffed with industry secondees is a captured board, at which point the program fails its own test and I would say so. Write it that way and the Speaker B has described how to draft the statute, not a reason to reject the trade.

Speaker C [opening]: Let me state the strongest version of each position on the table, because the disagreement here is narrower and sharper than it appears. The Speaker A's argument is not a plea for a shield — it is an engineering claim. Continuous hardware attestation on live production inference is the deepest instrumentation any American regulator has ever asked for. Attach that depth of visibility to unbounded exposure, and you get concealment, offshoring, and logs written to be unreadable. They are also right that fault-based tort collapses in asynchronous multi-agent workflows: three vendors, a fine-tune, and an apportionment doctrine with no tested application to chained models. A no-fault door is a real answer to that. The Speaker B's argument is equally serious and cuts the other way: the shield is self-executing statutory text, while the remedy is delegated to an agency. HHS narrowed the Vaccine Injury Table by rulemaking in 1995, stripping residual seizure disorder off the schedule, and claimants absorbed it. The protection is permanent; the compensation is revisable. Both positions hold simultaneously only if one thing is true — that a solvent payer produces the same corrective pressure as an accountable author. It does not. That is the fault line.

The draft writes the state-of-the-art defense into federal statute and generalizes it across an entire industry. Products liability spent a century establishing that a regulator's floor is not a manufacturer's ceiling. Wyeth v. Levine, 2009: FDA-approved labeling did not preempt a state failure-to-warn claim, and Diana Levine kept her judgment after losing an arm. Riegel v. Medtronic, 2008, went the other way for premarket-approved devices — and produced a category where the agency's judgment became the only judgment an injured patient could ever invoke. This proposal builds Riegel for every covered AI system. My amendment is one sentence: invert the tier function. Tier compliance should never bar recovery. Tier status and demonstrated system properties should calibrate enhanced damages upward against the non-compliant. Tiers are either the minimum below which you are exposed, or the maximum above which you are safe. This draft makes them the second. Congress should make them the first.

The Speaker A's load-bearing premise — that no US regulator has obtained inspection at this depth without a corresponding liability limit — is not supported by the American record, and they were honest enough to invite the counterexample. The FDA runs post-market adverse-event reporting, facility inspection, and mandatory recall authority over an industry carrying full product liability everywhere outside the narrow 1986 vaccine carve-out. Sarbanes-Oxley went further in 2002: sections 302 and 906 extracted personal certification of internal controls from named CEOs and CFOs under criminal penalty, with no liability limitation whatsoever, from an industry that fought harder than this one is fighting telemetry. What was missing before Enron was not corporate immunity. It was a signature. I will narrow my claim honestly: FDA inspection is periodic and document-based, not continuous attested inference logging. So the burden sits with the affirmative to name what makes continuous attestation categorically different — other than cost. And I will name the weakness on my own side. Regulators under-enforce for reasons of appropriations and capture at least as much as liability exposure, so certification alone carries none of this on its back.

The one point the Speaker B and the Speaker A converged on — parent-company joint enterprise liability plus compulsory insurance — secures a payer and binds no human to a standard before harm. In the multi-vendor chain the Speaker A described, every disclosed party is reachable and every disclosed party disclaims the design choice. Corporate revocation, artifact destruction, even disgorgement never reach the person who set the threshold. So condition any liability limitation on named-officer certification of the tier claim, on the Sarbanes-Oxley template. I will concede the obvious objection before it is made: two decades of section 906 certifications produced very few prosecutions, and firms will appoint a Chief AI Compliance Officer to absorb the signature. Certification's value is evidentiary, not deterrent. It creates a dated, attributable representation that a forensic body can subpoena. That is a weaker claim than deterrence, and I am making the weaker claim deliberately. Meanwhile the deterrence channel in this entire proposal runs through a filed claim — and the tenant screening, credit scoring, resume filtering, and Medicaid eligibility errors the Speaker B catalogued are visible only in aggregate. The rejected applicant never learns why. A no-fault door helps only the claimant who knows they were injured. So the statute needs proactive audit and public enforcement that fire when nobody files. And it needs a bounded carve-out: no liability limitation for death, permanent physical disability, or irrecoverable financial and custodial loss. An unbounded exclusion swallows the bargain and I will not demand one. But you cannot sell immunity against a loss you cannot price.

One technical gap in this draft has gone untouched, and it determines whether the whole bargain is real. Attestation proves that a specific binary ran on a specific device and that a log was not altered. Tier placement prices something else entirely — group error disparity, robustness under distribution shift, failure behavior at the tails. If the verification layer cannot certify the properties the tier claims, Congress grants a shield against an unverified representation. I will state my exposure openly: if the affirmative produces signed, reproducible evaluation runs binding model weights to held-out disparity and robustness results, attestation reaches a meaningful slice of that property space and my sequencing demand weakens. That is the question this debate should resolve, and I am not pretending it is settled. The constructive path is sequencing: excise receipts fund interpretability capacity and independent forensic staffing first, and immunity switches on only for properties verification demonstrably reaches. One structural condition makes all of it work. This draft puts tier assignment, compliance verification, and claim adjudication inside a single board — the same entity sets the price of immunity, audits whether it was earned, and pays when it was not. Separate those three functions into three bodies with different incentives and different appropriations. If Congress will not fund that separation, then the Speaker B's simpler instruction is the better statute: strike the immunity clause and keep the rest. A shield issued by a captured board is not a bargain. It is a transfer.
